title: Will regular users adapt?
hook: An explicit adaptation model treats new and returning users differently.

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: regular users at first resist a better design because they're used to the old one.

misconception: Treating primacy effect as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: regular users at first resist a better design because they're used to the old one.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: Returning users follow the toy lift L(t)=5−15 exp(−t/3), in percentage points; new users stay at +5. What returning-user lift is expected on day 9?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-primacy-effect/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Returning user lift L(t)=5-15exp(-t/3)pp; new users always5pp. Returningday0=-10,day3≈-.518,day9≈4.253. Compare adaptation with persistent harm assumptions.

claims.text: Returning users retain day-nine lift 4.253 points; new users retain 5. The stipulated adaptation penalty starts large and then decays.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-primacy-effect/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Returning user lift L(t)=5-15exp(-t/3)pp; new users always5pp. Returningday0=-10,day3≈-.518,day9≈4.253. Compare adaptation with persistent harm assumptions.

claims.text: Early harm can coexist with later gains under this model. An observed early loss does not prove adaptation, though: persistent harm is a competing explanation that needs longer follow-up and an appropriate comparison.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-primacy-effect/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Returning user lift L(t)=5-15exp(-t/3)pp; new users always5pp. Returningday0=-10,day3≈-.518,day9≈4.253. Compare adaptation with persistent harm assumptions.

claims.text: An early returning-user loss becomes a later gain. Does that alone prove adaptation caused it? Time patterns can fit several mechanisms, including changing user mix or other concurrent changes.
